short: In one reign Japan went from a closed feudal order to an industrial power that defeated Russia.
full:
Mutsuhito acceded in February 1867 at fourteen, a year before the decree that abolished the shogunate in his name. He moved from the seclusion of the Kyoto palace to Tokyo, appeared in Western military uniform, and was made the visible centre of a state that his ministers — Ōkubo, Kido, Itō, Yamagata — actually ran. How much he decided himself remains debated; he was consulted constantly and rarely overruled his cabinet in public.

The changes made under his name were total. Domains became prefectures in 1871, conscription replaced the samurai in 1873, and railways, telegraphs, banks, compulsory schooling and a European legal code followed. The 1889 constitution and the Diet elected the next year gave Japan the first parliamentary government in Asia, with the emperor sovereign above it. Victory over China in 1895 and over Russia in 1905 brought Taiwan, southern Sakhalin and, in 1910, the annexation of Korea. When he died on 30 July 1912, Japan had gone in forty-five years from imposed unequal treaties to a recognised imperial power.
